2
A particle travels in a straight line with speed v.
v .
The particle slows down and changes direction. The new speed of the particle is 2
v in the same direction as the initial path of the particle.
The new velocity has a component of 4
Through which angle has the particle turned?
A
27°
B
30°
C
45°
D
60°

hints: Call the turn angle $\theta$ measured from the original straight-line direction, so the given $\frac{v}{4}$ is the adjacent side for that angle.
For a velocity of magnitude $\frac{v}{2}$ at angle $\theta$, the component along the original direction is $\frac{v}{2}\cos\theta$.
Set $\frac{v}{2}\cos\theta = \frac{v}{4}$, cancel $v$, then find the angle whose cosine is $\frac{1}{2}$.
walkthrough: Take the initial direction as the reference axis. Let $\theta$ be the angle the new velocity has turned away from this axis.
The component of a vector along a direction is magnitude times cosine of the angle to that direction, so forward component $= \text{(new speed)}\cos\theta$.

A.explanation: This does not satisfy $\cos\theta = 1/2$. It may come from an incorrect inverse-trigonometry step.

B.explanation: This would need a forward component of $\frac{v}{2}\cos30^{\circ}$, which is larger than the given $\frac{v}{4}$.

C.explanation: This would need a forward component of $\frac{v}{2}\cos45^{\circ}$, which is larger than the given $\frac{v}{4}$.

D.explanation: The forward component is half the new speed, so $\cos\theta = 1/2$ and $\theta = 60^{\circ}$.
